mainTopic: When the מבול began (רבי אליעזר vs. רבי יהושע), and א' תשרי as the new year for vegetables and tithes
overview: This amud finishes the מחלוקת between רבי אליעזר (the מבול began in מרחשון) and רבי יהושע (it began in אייר). רבי יהושע says that because people changed their ways, הקב"ה changed nature and brought rain in the dry season. The גמרא asks two questions on רבי אליעזר. First, how is מרחשון the 'second month'? Answer: it is second after תשרי, the month of judgment. Second, what was 'changed' if rain falls in מרחשון anyway? Answer: following רב חסדא, the flood waters were boiling hot, as shown by the word 'שכך' (cooled down). A ברייתא then rules that Jewish sages count the flood like רבי אליעזר and the sun-and-moon cycles like רבי יהושע. Next the גמרא returns to the משנה's 'new year for vegetables'. It explains that this means the rabbinic vegetable tithe, distinguishes it from the Torah tithe, and explains why the words 'tithes' and 'vegetables' are plural. The amud ends with a new ברייתא about picking vegetables on ערב ראש השנה, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: God changed nature because the people changed their ways
steps.stepSummary: The end of רבי יהושע's statement: because the generation changed its behavior, הקב"ה changed the natural order. He raised מזל כימה by day, removed two of its stars, and brought the מבול.
steps.simpleTranslation: But because they changed their actions, the Holy One, Blessed be He, changed the acts of Creation for them. He made the constellation כימה rise during the day, took away two stars, and brought a flood to the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing רבי יהושע's statement that the מבול began in אייר. He explains that the flood was a deliberate change to how nature normally works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In אייר, כימה normally sets during the day and the springs dry up, so rain does not usually come. רבי יהושע says that because the people changed their deeds, הקב"ה changed nature to match: He raised כימה by day and pulled out two stars, which let the flood waters loose. This idea of 'changing' nature is exactly what the גמרא will question next on רבי אליעזר's view.

keyTerms.meaning: The acts of Creation; the natural order of the world
The constellation כימה (often identified as the Pleiades)
The Flood in the time of נח

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new statement. It is the end of רבי יהושע's statement from the previous lines, so it supports the view that the flood began in אייר.

phrases.english: But because they changed their actions,
the Holy One, Blessed be He, changed for them
phrases.notes: Measure for measure: they changed, so He changed.

phrases.english: the acts of Creation,
and He made the constellation Kima rise during the day,
phrases.notes: In אייר, כימה normally sets during the daytime.

phrases.english: and He took away two stars
phrases.notes: Two stars were removed from כימה.

phrases.english: and He brought a flood to the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבי יהושע's statement, which began on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהושע, the flood in אייר was an unnatural change to Creation, a response to the people changing their deeds.

steps.title: How does 'second month' fit רבי אליעזר?
steps.stepSummary: The verse says the flood began in the 'second month.' Counting from ניסן, that is אייר, which fits רבי יהושע. For רבי אליעזר, who says מרחשון, what does 'second' mean?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for רבי יהושע, because the verse says 'second' month. But for רבי אליעזר, what does 'second' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אליעזר from the wording of the פסוק 'in the second month.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Months are usually counted from ניסן, so the 'second month' is אייר, which matches רבי יהושע perfectly. מרחשון is the eighth month from ניסן, so the verse seems to contradict רבי אליעזר.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted, it makes sense (for one view)
This is why it is written

phrases.english: Granted, according to Rabbi Yehoshua,
this is why it is written: "second" month.
phrases.notes: אייר is the second month counting from ניסן.

phrases.english: But according to Rabbi Eliezer,
what is the meaning of "second"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that both views have been stated, the גמרא tests רבי אליעזר's view against the verse.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אליעזר's view that the flood began in מרחשון
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse calls the month 'second.' Counting from ניסן, that is אייר, not מרחשון.

steps.title: Second to the month of judgment
steps.stepSummary: For רבי אליעזר, 'second' means the second month after תשרי, the month of judgment. That month is מרחשון.
steps.simpleTranslation: It means second to the month of judgment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רבי אליעזר by counting the months from a different starting point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If you count from תשרי, the month of judgment (ראש השנה), מרחשון is indeed the second month. So the verse fits רבי אליעזר too; the two views simply count from different starting months.

keyTerms.meaning: Second to the (month of) judgment, i.e., the month after תשרי
Judgment (referring to ראש השנה in תשרי)

steps.whyThisMatters: This ties back to the larger debate in this סוגיא about whether the world's year starts from תשרי or from ניסן.

phrases.english: Second to the month of judgment.
phrases.notes: Second after תשרי, which is מרחשון.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the verse (a different starting point for counting months)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We assumed 'second' was counted from ניסן, which pointed to אייר.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Second' can be counted from תשרי, which points to מרחשון.

steps.title: For רבי אליעזר, what was 'changed'?
steps.stepSummary: For רבי יהושע, rain in אייר is unnatural, so הקב"ה really 'changed' Creation. For רבי אליעזר, rain in מרחשון is normal, so what was changed?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for רבי יהושע: this is how He 'changed' nature. But for רבי אליעזר, what did He change?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a second challenge to רבי אליעזר, this time about the idea that nature was 'changed.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: אייר is the dry season, so a flood then is clearly a change in nature. מרחשון is the rainy season, so heavy rain then seems ordinary, and it is unclear what was changed.

phrases.english: Granted, according to Rabbi Yehoshua,
this is how He changed nature.
phrases.notes: Rain does not normally fall in אייר.

phrases.english: But according to Rabbi Eliezer,
what did He change?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to רבי אליעזר, built on the 'changed Creation' language of step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the flood involved a change in nature, according to רבי אליעזר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Rain in the rainy season is not a change in nature, so the word 'שינה' does not seem to fit.

steps.title: The change was boiling water, following רב חסדא
steps.stepSummary: The answer follows רב חסדא: they sinned with 'boiling heat' and were punished with 'boiling heat.' The flood waters themselves were scalding hot, and that was the change.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like רב חסדא's teaching. רב חסדא said: with boiling they sinned, and with boiling they were punished.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רבי אליעזר. Even in the rainy season there was a real change, because the flood water was boiling hot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The change was not the timing of the rain but its nature: hot, scalding water instead of normal rain. This fits a measure-for-measure pattern: a burning sin earns a burning punishment.

phrases.english: In accordance with Rav Chisda.
As Rav Chisda said:
With boiling heat they sinned
and with boiling heat they were punished.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The only possible 'change' was rain falling in the wrong season.
steps.terutzMaskana: The change was the temperature of the water: the flood waters were boiling hot.

steps.title: Explaining both halves and proving the water was hot
steps.stepSummary: The 'boiling' sin is עריות, sexual sin. The proof of the boiling punishment is a גזירה שוה: 'וישכו המים' (the waters abated) uses the same root as 'וחמת המלך שככה' (the king's fury cooled), which shows the waters had been hot.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'They sinned with boiling' means with sin. 'They were punished with boiling': it is written here, 'And the waters abated,' and it is written there, 'And the fury of the king abated.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains each half of רב חסדא's statement and proves from פסוקים that the flood waters were hot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'שכך' in אסתר describes the king's hot anger cooling down. Using it for the flood waters shows they too were 'hot' and later cooled. That proves the flood was scalding water, which is the change answering רבי אליעזר's problem.

keyTerms.meaning: Through sin (here, the 'heated' sin of עריות)
It is written here... and it is written there (formula for a גזירה שוה)

steps.whatToRemember: Both views fit the verses. 'Second month' is counted from ניסן (רבי יהושע) or from תשרי (רבי אליעזר). The 'change' in nature is either rain in the dry season (רבי יהושע) or boiling-hot rain (רבי אליעזר, via רב חסדא).

phrases.english: "They sinned with boiling heat" means through sin,
phrases.notes: The heated sin of forbidden relations.

phrases.english: and "they were punished with boiling heat":
It is written here: "And the waters abated" (Bereishis 8:1),
and it is written there: "And the fury of the king abated" (Esther 7:10).
phrases.notes: 'Abated' means cooled down, so the waters had been hot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains and proves רב חסדא's statement used in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That the flood waters were boiling hot
steps.raayaSupportSource: A גזירה שוה between 'וישכו המים' (בראשית ח:א) and 'וחמת המלך שככה' (אסתר ז:י)

steps.title: How the sages actually count: the flood like רבי אליעזר, the seasons like רבי יהושע
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records how the two opinions are used in practice. Jewish sages count the flood like רבי אליעזר (from תשרי) and the seasonal cycles like רבי יהושע (from ניסן). Non-Jewish sages count even the flood like רבי יהושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: The Jewish sages count the years of the flood like רבי אליעזר, and the cycles of the seasons like רבי יהושע. The sages of the other nations count even the flood like רבי יהושע.
steps.whatsHappening: After all the back-and-forth about רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע, the גמרא brings a ברייתא that tells us which view is used for which kind of counting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two views are not simply picked between. Each one is used for a different kind of calculation. For dating history (the flood, the years since Creation), Jewish sages start from תשרי. For calculating the cycles of the sun and moon (תקופה), they start from ניסן.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Rabbis taught.' This opens a ברייתא.
The flood in the time of נח.
A season or cycle, used for calculating the sun and moon.
The sages of the other nations of the world.

steps.whatToRemember: In practice we use both views. History, such as the flood, is counted from תשרי (רבי אליעזר). The cycles of the sun and moon are counted from ניסן (רבי יהושע).
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think one opinion simply 'won.' Each opinion is used, but for a different kind of counting.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
The Jewish sages count the years for the flood
phrases.notes: They count the dates of the flood and of Creation.

phrases.english: like Rabbi Eliezer (from Tishrei),
and for the cycle of seasons, like Rabbi Yehoshua (from Nisan).
The sages of the nations of the world
count even the flood like Rabbi Yehoshua.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מוֹנִין לַמַּבּוּל כְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the רבי אליעזר / רבי יהושע section by stating how each view is applied in practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Jewish sages count the flood from תשרי and the seasonal cycles from ניסן. Non-Jewish sages count the flood from ניסן as well.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: the new year for vegetables, with a ברייתא's longer list
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words 'and for vegetables.' It then brings a ברייתא that says א' תשרי is the new year for vegetables, for tithes, and for vows.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And for vegetables' (the words of the משנה). A ברייתא teaches: the first of תשרי is the new year for vegetables, for tithes, and for vows.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting the next phrase of the משנה. It brings a ברייתא with a longer list, and this sets up the questions that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה only says 'vegetables.' The ברייתא adds 'tithes' and 'vows.' Listing both 'vegetables' and 'tithes' will raise the question of why they are listed separately.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It was taught.' This introduces a ברייתא.
Tithes, the portions separated from produce.

phrases.english: "And for vegetables" (quoting the Mishnah).
phrases.notes: Quoting the משנה: א' תשרי is the new year for vegetables.

phrases.english: It was taught in a Baraita: for vegetables,
and for tithes, and for vows.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section of the משנה, moving from the flood discussion to the new year for vegetables.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: א' תשרי is the new year for vegetables, tithes, and vows.

steps.title: What does 'for vegetables' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the new year 'for vegetables' refers to.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'For vegetables': what is this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a simple clarifying question. Which law about vegetables does this new year affect?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'new year for vegetables' does not tell us which law is involved. The גמרא wants the exact meaning before going further.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What are they?' This asks for a definition.

phrases.english: "For vegetables": what is this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of a term in the ברייתא and משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which law is governed by the 'new year for vegetables.'

steps.title: It means the vegetable tithe
steps.stepSummary: 'For vegetables' means מעשר ירק, the tithe taken from vegetables.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is the vegetable tithe.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the new year for vegetables is about separating tithes from vegetables.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vegetables picked before א' תשרי and vegetables picked after it belong to different years. You may not tithe from one year's vegetables for the other year's vegetables.

keyTerms.meaning: The tithe on vegetables. It is rabbinic (דרבנן).

phrases.english: The vegetable tithe.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.

steps.title: Isn't that the same as 'tithes'?
steps.stepSummary: If 'vegetables' means a tithe, then it seems the same as the next item, 'tithes.' So why does the ברייתא list both?
steps.simpleTranslation: That is the same as 'tithes'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer. If 'vegetables' is about tithing, the ברייתא seems to repeat itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists 'vegetables' and 'tithes' as two separate items. If both are about tithes, one looks extra.

keyTerms.meaning: 'That is the same as...' This points out a repetition.

phrases.english: Isn't this the same as "tithes"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the definition given in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's listing of both 'vegetables' and 'tithes.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'vegetables' means tithes, the item 'tithes' is a repetition.

steps.title: One is a rabbinic tithe, the other a Torah tithe
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא first taught the rabbinic tithe (vegetables). Then it taught the Torah tithe (grain, wine, and oil).
steps.simpleTranslation: It taught the rabbinic one, and then it teaches the Torah one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two items are different kinds of tithe, so nothing is repeated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מעשר ירק is only דרבנן. 'Tithes' means the Torah tithe on grain, wine, and oil. The ברייתא tells us א' תשרי is the new year for both.

phrases.english: It taught the one that is rabbinic
and then it teaches the one that is from the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 11.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both items are the same tithe, so one is extra.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Vegetables' is the rabbinic tithe and 'tithes' is the Torah tithe.

steps.title: Why not list the Torah tithe first?
steps.stepSummary: If so, the ברייתא should have listed the more important Torah tithe first.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it teach the Torah one first!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the order of the ברייתא. Normally the Torah law would come first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since דאורייתא is the more basic and stronger law, it seems it should come before the rabbinic one.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Let it teach.' This suggests a better way the text could have been written.

phrases.english: Then let it teach the Torah one first!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the order implied by the answer in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The order of items in the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Torah law is more basic and should be listed before rabbinic law.

steps.title: It was dear to him, so he put it first
steps.stepSummary: Because the vegetable tithe was dear to the תנא, he mentioned it first.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since it was dear to him, he put it first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the תנא chose to put the rabbinic tithe first because it was especially beloved to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rabbinic rule is the newer point, the bigger חידוש. That made it dear to the תנא, so he opened with it before the Torah tithe.

phrases.english: Since it was dear to him,
he put it first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 13.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Torah law should always come first.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rabbinic tithe was put first because it was dear to the תנא.

steps.title: And what about our משנה, which mentions only vegetables?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why our משנה mentions only vegetables and leaves out the Torah tithe.
steps.simpleTranslation: And our תנא (of the משנה)?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns back to our משנה. It lists only 'vegetables,' so why does it leave out the Torah tithes?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists both kinds of tithe. Our משנה mentions only the rabbinic one, so the גמרא wants to know how the Torah tithe is covered.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Our תנא,' meaning the author of our משנה.

phrases.english: And our Tanna (of the Mishnah), why did he leave out the Torah tithe?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from explaining the ברייתא to explaining our משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why our משנה mentions only vegetables and not the Torah tithe.
steps.kashyaTarget: Our משנה, which lists only 'vegetables' and leaves out the Torah tithe that the ברייתא lists.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If א' תשרי is also the new year for the Torah tithe, as the ברייתא says, our משנה seems incomplete for not mentioning it.

steps.title: If the rabbinic tithe follows תשרי, the Torah tithe surely does
steps.stepSummary: Our משנה taught the rabbinic tithe. We learn the Torah tithe from it, all the more so.
steps.simpleTranslation: It taught the rabbinic one, and all the more so the Torah one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that our משנה did not need to mention the Torah tithe. If even the rabbinic tithe goes by א' תשרי, the Torah tithe certainly does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a כל שכן argument: the weaker, rabbinic case teaches us about the stronger, Torah case. So mentioning only vegetables covers both.
steps.whatToRemember: א' תשרי is the new year for both the rabbinic vegetable tithe and the Torah tithe on grain, wine, and oil. Our משנה mentions only vegetables, and the Torah tithe is learned from it with a כל שכן.

phrases.english: He taught the rabbinic one,
and all the more so the Torah one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Our משנה left out the Torah tithe.
steps.terutzMaskana: Teaching the rabbinic tithe already includes the Torah tithe, all the more so.

steps.title: Why does the text say tithes in the plural?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא says 'tithes' (plural) instead of just 'tithe' (singular).
steps.simpleTranslation: But let it say 'tithe' (singular)!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא looks closely at one word in the ברייתא and asks why it is plural. It wants to know what the plural form is coming to add.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said ראש השנה is the new year 'for tithes.' One kind of tithe would only need the singular word 'tithe.' So the plural must be hinting at more than one kind of מעשר.

keyTerms.meaning: But let it teach (why didn't it say it this way?)
A tithe, a tenth set aside from produce or animals

phrases.english: But let it teach: 'Tithe' (singular)!
phrases.notes: The ברייתא actually said 'tithes' in the plural.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues looking closely at the ברייתא's wording after the question about the order in which it listed things was settled.
steps.kashyaTarget: The plural word 'tithes' in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If only one kind of tithe were meant, the singular would be enough. So the plural looks like an extra word.

steps.title: The plural includes two kinds of tithe
steps.stepSummary: The plural includes both the animal tithe and the grain tithe.
steps.simpleTranslation: It means both the animal tithe and the grain tithe.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'tithes' is plural because two different tithes are included: מעשר בהמה and מעשר דגן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plural is not an extra word. It tells us that the first of תשרי is the new year for both tithes. This fits the opinion that the new year for מעשר בהמה is also א׳ תשרי.

keyTerms.meaning: The tithe of animals: every tenth newborn animal is set aside
The tithe of grain (here meaning crop produce)
Both this one and that one

phrases.english: Both the animal tithe
and the grain tithe.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶחָד מַעְשַׂר בְּהֵמָה וְאֶחָד מַעְשַׂר דָּגָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the plural word 'tithes.'
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the plural by showing that two separate categories are included
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The plural seemed to be an unnecessary extra word.
steps.terutzMaskana: The plural covers both מעשר בהמה and מעשר דגן.

steps.title: Why does the text say vegetables in the plural?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the text says 'vegetables' (plural) instead of 'vegetable' (singular).
steps.simpleTranslation: But let it say 'vegetable' (singular)!
steps.whatsHappening: Using the same kind of question as before, the גמרא now asks why vegetables are written in the plural.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vegetables are one category of produce, so the singular word would seem to be enough. The גמרא wants to know what the plural adds.

phrases.english: But let it teach: 'Vegetable' (singular)!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same kind of question it just asked about 'tithes,' now applied to 'vegetables.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If vegetables are a single category, the singular would be enough.

steps.title: Two kinds of vegetables with two tithing moments
steps.stepSummary: The plural hints at two kinds of vegetables, as a משנה teaches: bundled ones and unbundled ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: There are two kinds of vegetables, as we learned in a משנה: a vegetable that is usually tied in bundles becomes subject to tithing once it is bundled. One that is not bundled becomes subject to tithing once a person fills a container with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'vegetables' is plural because there are two kinds of vegetables. It brings a משנה as its source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some vegetables are sold tied in bundles, and their processing is finished once they are bundled. Others are not bundled, and their processing is finished once a container is filled. The plural tells us that the ראש השנה rule covers both kinds, even though each kind has a different finishing point.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה
From when one fills the container

steps.confusionAlert: The two moments in this משנה are not about which year the vegetable belongs to. They are about when the vegetable's processing counts as finished, so that it must be tithed. Which year a vegetable belongs to is decided by when it was picked, as the next ברייתא shows.

phrases.english: There are two kinds of vegetables,
as we learned: a vegetable that is usually bundled — from when it is bundled;
phrases.notes: From then it is subject to tithing.

phrases.english: and one that is not bundled — from when he fills the container.

steps.terutzMaskana: The plural covers both bundled and unbundled vegetables, which become subject to tithing at different points.
steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא explains every plural: 'tithes' means מעשר בהמה plus מעשר דגן, and 'vegetables' means bundled plus unbundled vegetables.

steps.title: New ברייתא: picking vegetables before and after sunset on the eve of ראש השנה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא begins describing a person who picked vegetables before sunset on ערב ראש השנה and then picked more.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: If someone picked vegetables on ערב ראש השנה before the sun set, and then he went back and picked more...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא, and the case is still being set up. It continues on the next amud, where we will hear what the ruling is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vegetables picked before sunset belong to the old year. The ones picked afterward will belong to the new year. This sets up a practical case where vegetables from two different years are mixed together, and you may not tithe from one year's crop to cover another's.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
If one picked vegetables on the eve of Rosh HaShana
before the sun set,
and then he went back and picked more
